text: This is the capstone for Chapter Six. We're going to take one complete, realistic T-SQL stored procedure and translate it into idiomatic PL-SQL, line by line, calling out every single decision point along the way, using everything this chapter has covered.

Here's the starting point. Get customer order summary takes a customer I-D, checks the order count, prints a message and returns early if there are none, and otherwise returns the full order list as a result set. A completely ordinary, everyday T-SQL pattern.

First two decisions. At customer I-D int becomes p underscore customer underscore id, in number — no at sign, an explicit direction, and a p underscore prefix by convention. And every declare at var scattered through the body gets collected into one declare section, or I-S for a named procedure, before begin. That's the block structure from Lesson 35, doing real work.

Third decision: if at order count equals zero, begin, print, return, end — becomes if v order count equals zero then, DBMS output put line, return, end if. Print becomes DBMS output put line, and end if, two words, is always required, no matter how many statements are inside.

Fourth decision, and the biggest one: that final bare select, which just streams back to the caller for free in T-SQL, has no PL-SQL equivalent at all. The procedure's own signature has to change, adding a sys ref cursor out parameter, opened for the query instead of just running it bare. That's Lesson 38, directly in action.

And one more addition worth making even though the original didn't have it: an exception section with a when others handler. The T-SQL version had no try catch, but a production quality PL-SQL translation should be defensive here — it costs nothing, and an unhandled PL-SQL exception behaves differently from an unhandled T-SQL error.

That closes out Chapter Six. You now know PL-SQL's block structure, packages, anonymous blocks, REF CURSORs, collections, autonomous transactions, and bulk operations — the concepts that genuinely don't map one to one onto T-SQL. Next up, Chapter Seven: MySQL's SQL mode, and why flipping one setting changes how MySQL behaves out from under you. See you there.
